steps.title: Understand what a buck converter does
steps.objective: Understand that a buck converter steps a higher DC voltage down to a lower DC voltage efficiently.
steps.task: In your own words: why can't you just use a resistor to drop 12V to 3.3V for a circuit that draws real current?

hints.1: Think about what happens to the extra 8.7V if you just used a resistor, where does that energy go?
hints.2: Power dissipated as heat scales with current. What happens as the load draws more current?
hints.3: Look at Section 7.3, Feature Description, for how the regulator switches instead of dropping voltage linearly.
hints.4: A resistor wastes the voltage difference as heat, and that waste gets worse as current increases. A buck converter switches the input on and off rapidly and stores energy in an inductor, so almost no energy is wasted — that's why it's efficient at any load current.

steps.title: Regulator IC: TPS54331
steps.objective: Understand why a specific buck regulator IC is chosen for this voltage/current range.
steps.task: We're using the TPS54331 with a 12V input. Looking at its Electrical Characteristics table, what's the typical current limit threshold?

hints.1: Check the Electrical Characteristics table — current limit is listed with min/typ/max values.
hints.2: Look for a row labeled 'Current limit threshold' near the switching specs.
hints.3: Check Section 6.5, Electrical Characteristics, for the typical current limit value at VIN = 12V.
hints.4: The TPS54331 has a typical current limit threshold of 5.8A at VIN = 12V, well above what our 3.3V/3A output needs, which gives design headroom before the regulator's protection kicks in.

steps.title: Place the regulator IC
steps.objective: Place the TPS54331 on the schematic and identify its key pins.
steps.task: Place the TPS54331 IC on the canvas. Which pin should VIN (12V) connect to?

expected_answer.reasoning_prompt: You placed the IC. Now: which pin number is VIN, and why isn't it Pin 1?
reasoning_key_ideas: Pin 1 is BOOT, used for the internal gate-drive bootstrap capacitor, not the input rail
VIN feeds the internal power switch that performs the actual buck conversion

reasoning_hints.1: Look closely at the pin numbering in the datasheet's pin diagram — it's easy to assume Pin 1 is the input.
reasoning_hints.2: Pin 1 has a completely different job related to driving the internal switch, not receiving input power.
reasoning_hints.3: Check Section 9.1, Pin Configuration, and read what Pin 1 (BOOT) is actually used for.
reasoning_hints.4: Pin 2 is VIN — that's where your 12V input rail connects, feeding the internal power switch. Pin 1 is BOOT, used only for the internal gate-drive bootstrap capacitor that helps switch the high-side FET on and off.

hints.1: The pin name usually tells you exactly what it's for.
hints.2: Look for a pin literally labeled VIN on the package diagram.
hints.3: Check Section 9.1, Pin Configuration, for the pin numbering and names.
hints.4: Pin 2 VIN is where your 12V input rail connects - Pin 1 is BOOT0, used for internal gate drive bootstrap capacitor, not the input rail, VIN feeds the internal power switch that does the actual buck conversion.

steps.title: Adding the input capacitor
steps.objective: Understand why an input capacitor is needed and place it correctly.
steps.task: In your own words, what are we adding here and why does it need to be there?

expected_answer.reasoning_prompt: Nice — you placed the input capacitor. Now: why does it need to sit right there, close to VIN?
reasoning_key_ideas: the input cap supplies the fast burst of current the switch needs the instant it turns on, faster than the source or a long trace can respond
it keeps VIN stable and reduces high-frequency ripple/noise created by the switching
it should be placed physically close to the IC's VIN and GND pins to minimize trace inductance

reasoning_hints.1: Think about what happens in the first microsecond the switch turns on — where does that sudden current come from?
reasoning_hints.2: The source (wall adapter, battery) can't respond instantly to a sudden current demand. What can, if it's close by?
reasoning_hints.3: Check Section 8.2, Typical Application, for why the input cap is placed immediately adjacent to VIN/GND.
reasoning_hints.4: The input capacitor acts as a local reservoir of charge that reacts instantly, supplying the sudden current pulses the switch demands so VIN doesn't sag or ring. It has to sit physically close to the pins so the current doesn't have to travel through a long, inductive trace.

hints.1: Think about what happens when the regulator suddenly draws a big pulse of current from the input, all at once.
hints.2: Look at what's connected directly between VIN and GND in the typical application circuit.
hints.3: Check Section 8.2, Typical Application, for the recommended input capacitance value.
hints.4: The input capacitor (typically 10µF ceramic) acts as a local energy reservoir, supplying the sudden current pulses the switching regulator demands so the input rail voltage doesn't sag or ring.

steps.title: Add the inductor
steps.objective: Understand the inductor's role in energy storage and place it between SW and the output.
steps.task: Place an inductor between the SW pin and the output node (VOUT).

expected_answer.reasoning_prompt: Why does the inductor go between SW and VOUT instead of just wiring SW straight to VOUT?
reasoning_key_ideas: the inductor stores energy while the switch is on and releases it while the switch is off
this turns the choppy on/off switched pulses at SW into a smooth, continuous current at VOUT
without it, VOUT would just be a squarewave-ish average of VIN, not a stable DC voltage

reasoning_hints.1: The SW pin isn't a steady voltage — it's a pulse train switching rapidly between VIN and ground. What would VOUT look like if it were wired straight to that?
reasoning_hints.2: Think about what component 'remembers' current flow and keeps it going even when the switch briefly turns off.
reasoning_hints.3: Check Section 8.2.2, Inductor Selection, for how the inductor's energy storage relates to output smoothness.
reasoning_hints.4: The inductor stores energy while SW is high and releases it smoothly while SW is low, averaging the choppy switched pulses into continuous current. Without it, VOUT would just be a noisy, unusable copy of the SW switching waveform instead of a steady DC voltage.

hints.1: The regulator doesn't just drop voltage, it switches a pin on and off rapidly. What component stores energy between switch pulses?
hints.2: Look at what connects the SW (switch) pin to the output side of the circuit.
hints.3: Check Section 8.2.2 for the inductor selection guidance and recommended value.
hints.4: The inductor stores energy while SW is on and releases it smoothly while SW is off, turning the choppy switched pulses into a steady output current — this is the core of how a buck converter works.

steps.title: Add the output capacitor
steps.objective: Understand why an output capacitor smooths the converted voltage.
steps.task: Place a capacitor between VOUT and GND.

expected_answer.reasoning_prompt: The inductor already smooths current — so why do we still need a capacitor here too?
reasoning_key_ideas: the inductor's output current still has some ripple, it's smoothed but not perfectly flat
the output capacitor filters that remaining ripple into a stable, clean DC voltage
it also helps supply/absorb sudden load current changes without VOUT dipping or spiking

reasoning_hints.1: 'Smoothed' doesn't mean perfectly flat — the inductor's current still has a small ripple riding on top of it.
reasoning_hints.2: What component is good at holding a steady voltage even when the current through it varies slightly?
reasoning_hints.3: Check Section 8.2.3, Output Capacitor Selection, for how it relates to output ripple voltage.
reasoning_hints.4: The inductor current still has ripple on it — the output capacitor filters that remaining ripple into a clean, stable 3.3V, and helps respond instantly if the load suddenly demands more or less current.

hints.1: The inductor's current isn't perfectly smooth, it ripples. What smooths a ripply voltage into something stable?
hints.2: Look at what's connected directly between VOUT and GND in the typical application circuit.
hints.3: Check Section 8.2.3 for output capacitance selection and ripple voltage targets.
hints.4: The output capacitor filters the remaining current ripple from the inductor, holding VOUT steady at 3.3V instead of a wavy approximation of it.

steps.title: Build the feedback network
steps.objective: Understand how the regulator senses output voltage to regulate it, via a resistor divider to FB.
steps.task: Place two resistors as a voltage divider from VOUT to GND, with the midpoint connected to the FB pin.

expected_answer.reasoning_prompt: Why does FB need a scaled-down version of VOUT instead of just seeing the full 3.3V directly?
reasoning_key_ideas: the IC's FB pin compares against a fixed small internal reference voltage (around 0.8V), not 3.3V
R1/R2 form a divider that scales VOUT down so the midpoint matches that reference when VOUT is correct
the IC adjusts its switching duty cycle based on that comparison to keep VOUT locked at 3.3V

reasoning_hints.1: The FB pin isn't comparing against 3.3V internally — it has its own fixed, much smaller reference voltage.
reasoning_hints.2: What do two resistors in series, tapped in the middle, let you do to a voltage?
reasoning_hints.3: Check Section 8.2.4, Feedback Resistor Selection, for the divider ratio formula and the internal reference value.
reasoning_hints.4: R1 and R2 scale VOUT down so the FB node sits at the IC's internal reference (about 0.8V) exactly when VOUT is 3.3V. The IC compares FB to that reference and speeds up or slows down switching to correct any drift.

hints.1: The regulator needs to know what the output voltage actually is, in order to correct it. How would you measure a voltage using only resistors?
hints.2: Look at the FB pin, what two components typically connect to it from VOUT and GND?
hints.3: Check Section 8.2.4 or the Feedback Resistor Selection section for the divider ratio formula.
hints.4: R1 and R2 form a voltage divider that scales VOUT down to the IC's internal reference voltage (typically 0.8V). The IC compares FB against that reference and adjusts switching to hold VOUT at exactly 3.3V.

steps.title: Review the completed schematic
steps.objective: Confirm the full signal path makes sense end-to-end.
steps.task: Trace the full path: what happens to current from VIN to VOUT, in order?

key_ideas: feedback resistors report VOUT back to FB
IC adjusts switching duty cycle to hold 3.3V

hints.1: Walk the schematic left to right: VIN → IC → SW → ... → VOUT. What's each stop doing?
hints.2: Don't forget the feedback loop, it's not just left-to-right, there's a path going backward too.
hints.3: Re-read Section 8.1, Overview, which usually summarizes the whole control loop in a few sentences.
hints.4: 12V enters at VIN. The IC rapidly switches the SW pin on/off. The inductor and output capacitor turn those pulses into a smooth 3.3V. The feedback resistors sample that 3.3V and report it to FB, so the IC can keep adjusting its switching to hold the output steady even as load changes.
